Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell $K=[a,b]=[x_j,x_{j+1}]$ of length $h_K$. Its interpolant slope is $s_K=(u(b)-u(a))/h_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^bu'(t)\,dt$ by [F1].

For every $x\in K$, $u'(x)-s_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^b(u'(x)-u'(t))\,dt$. A second use of [F1] and then [F2] gives $|u'(x)-u'(t)|\le\|u''\|_\infty|x-t|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$, hence $|u'(x)-s_K|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$.

The continuous function $|u''|$ has a finite maximum by [F4]. On each open cell $K^\circ=(x_j,x_{j+1})$, $q=|u'-s_K|^2$ is continuous and hence measurable; define $q=0$ at the finitely many nodes. This gives a nonnegative measurable representative of the squared derivative error, bounded by the finite cell bounds in step 2.1. The Lebesgue interval-measure and monotonicity facts in [F3] give $\int_K|(u-I_hu)'|^2\le h_K^3\|u''\|_\infty^2$. The open cells are disjoint and their complement consists of finitely many nodes of Lebesgue measure zero. Finite additivity of the measure $E\mapsto\int_Eq$ from [F3], with zero contribution from the nodes where $q=0$, therefore identifies the global Lebesgue squared norm with the sum of these cell integrals. Using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_Kh_K=1$ gives $\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2^2\le h^2\|u''\|_\infty^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the estimate; endpoint values follow from the nodal definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does

(the sign function); both witnesses are on the

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\varphi$ by [F1]. The triangle inequality and step 1.1 give $\|v\|_2\le\|\varphi\|_2+\varepsilon\le\|\varphi'\|_2+\varepsilon\le\|v'\|_2+2\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every positive $\varepsilon$, $\|v\|_2\le\|v'\|_2$. By [F4], squaring and adding the derivative norm proves the $H^1$ estimate.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

If $\eta_h<\alpha$, then $\alpha-\eta_h>0$, so the inequality in step 1.1 is precisely coercivity with that constant. If $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then $\alpha-\eta_h\ge\alpha/2$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace over that same field: use [[def-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb C$. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite
length, including length zero, then $W$ is closed in $V$. This holds in ZF,
without a choice axiom; the ambient space need not be complete.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. In the **exact variational problem**, $V$ is a Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$), linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ is bounded and has the same linearity in its test argument as the second argument of $a$. Exact solutions satisfy $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. Boundedness and coercivity have the meanings in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].

For a **conforming perturbed Galerkin problem**, $V_h\subseteq V$ is a finite-dimensional subspace, $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ are the discrete form and load, and $u_h\in V_h$ solves $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$. Its discrete coercivity constant is any $\alpha_h>0$ such that $\operatorname{Re}a_h(w_h,w_h)\ge\alpha_h\|w_h\|_V^2$ for every $w_h\in V_h$. For $v_h\in V_h$, define

$$\delta_{a,h}(v_h):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V},\qquad \delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V}.$$

If $V_h=\{0\}$, both defects are defined to be zero. The load defect $\delta_{F,h}$ includes any source approximation or data oscillation; it is not assumed small or zero without a separate bound.

For a **nonconforming problem**, the exact space $V$ and finite-dimensional trial space $V_h$ need not satisfy $V_h\subseteq V$. Put $X_h:=V+V_h$ and equip it with a norm $\|\cdot\|_h$ whose restrictions to $V$ and $V_h$ are norms. The discrete form $a_h$ is defined on $V_h\times V_h$, and a bounded extension $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ means $\widetilde a_h=a_h$ on $V_h\times V_h$ and $|\widetilde a_h(z,w_h)|\le M_h\|z\|_h\|w_h\|_h$. For an exact solution $u\in V$, define the nonconforming consistency defect

$$\delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_h(u):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_h},$$

with value zero if $V_h=\{0\}$. This residual need not vanish: the exact weak equation is only asserted for tests in $V$.

The physical exact form on real-valued functions with square-integrable gradients is $a(U,W):=\int_\Omega\nabla U(x)^TA(x)\nabla W(x)\,dx$. The pulled-back exact tensor and form are

$$B_h(y):=J_h(y)D\Phi_h(y)^{-1}A(\Phi_h(y))D\Phi_h(y)^{-T},\qquad a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}(v,w):=\int_{\Omega_h}\nabla v(y)^T B_h(y)\nabla w(y)\,dy.$$

The **geometry-lifted form defect** is the difference between $a_h^{\mathrm{lift}}$ and the form using $\widetilde B_h$. No meshwise approximation rate is part of this definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$

   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric

3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the absolute value as in
[[def-abs-value]]. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$,

$$\|v\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

Consequently $\|v\|_{H^1(0,1)}\le\sqrt2\,\|v'\|_{L^2(0,1)}$.

Let $0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite interval partition, $h:=\max_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)$, and $u\in C^2([0,1])$. Let $I_hu$ be the continuous piecewise-linear function with nodal values $I_hu(x_j)=u(x_j)$. Then

$$\|(u-I_hu)'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

If $u(0)=u(1)=0$, then $I_hu$ also vanishes at both endpoints.

Let $0=x_0<\cdots<x_N=1$ be a finite partition with cell lengths $h_K$ and maximum $h$. Let $A\in C^2([0,1])$, and let $v_h,w_h$ be continuous piecewise-linear functions. Define the exact and midpoint stiffness forms by

$$a(v_h,w_h):=\sum_K\int_KA(x)v_h'(x)w_h'(x)\,dx,\qquad a_h(v_h,w_h):=\sum_Kh_KA(m_K)v_h'|_Kw_h'|_K,$$

where $m_K$ is the cell midpoint and the cell derivatives are constant. Then

$$|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|\le\frac{h^2}{24}\|A''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\|v_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\|w_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

The midpoint rule is exact for this stiffness integrand when $A$ is affine; for a general $C^2$ coefficient the displayed defect is retained. The bound is exact-arithmetic quadrature error, separate from roundoff.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|v'\|_2^2\le2\|v'\|_2^2$. Hence $a$ is bounded by $M$ in the $H^1$ norm and coercive with constant $\alpha/2$.

On each cell $K$, $A(m_K)\ge\alpha$, so $a_h(v_h,v_h)=\sum_Kh_KA(m_K)|v_h'|_K^2\ge\alpha\|v_h'\|_2^2$. By [F2], $\|v_h\|_{H^1}^2\le2\|v_h'\|_2^2$, hence $a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge(\alpha/2)\|v_h\|_{H^1}^2$ and $\alpha_h\ge\alpha/2$.
By [F3] and [F2], $\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt2\|(u-I_hu)'\|_2\le\sqrt2h\|u''\|_\infty$. Also the triangle inequality gives $\|(I_hu)'\|_2\le\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty$.

Apply [F5] with comparison function $I_hu$. Its best-approximation term is bounded by step 1.3; [F4] bounds its form defect by $C_Ah^2(\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty)/24$ because $\|w_h'\|_2\le\|w_h\|_{H^1}$. The load defect is exactly $\delta_{F,h}$ by [A1].
Substitute $M$ from step 1.1 and $\alpha_h\ge\alpha/2$ from step 1.2 into the first-Strang bound in step 2.1. This gives the displayed estimate and retains the full load defect.

Assume the hypotheses and notation of
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and
suppose additionally that $a$ is Hermitian:
$a(v,w)=\overline{a(w,v)}$. Then
$$\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$$
is the energy norm and the Galerkin solution is its best approximation:
$$\|u-u_h\|_a=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_a.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Put $e_h:=\widetilde u_h-u_h^G$. Use the discrete equation with test $e_h$ and the residual definition [A1] to obtain $\alpha_h\|e_h\|_V^2\le\operatorname{Re}a_h(e_h,e_h)=\operatorname{Re}(F_h(e_h)-a_h(u_h^G,e_h))\le\rho_h\|e_h\|_V$.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_k$. Assume its degrees of
freedom are bounded on $W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)$ for an integer
$\ell\ge1$, let $r,m\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\widehat I$ be its
interpolant. Thus
$\widehat Iq=q$ for $q\in\mathbb P_k$. On a shape-regular affine mesh
as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], for each cell $K$ with its
orientation-preserving reference map $F_K$ define
$$I_Kv=(\widehat I(v\circ F_K))\circ F_K^{-1}.$$
For every such cell, if $\ell\le r\le k+1$ and $0\le m\le r$, then for
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)}\le C h_K^{r-m}|v|_{W^{r,p}(K)}.$$
If $\ell>k+1$ and $0\le m\le k+1$, then for $v\in W^{\ell,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)} \le C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}h_K^{n-m}|v|_{W^{n,p}(K)}.$$
The constants are uniform over the mesh family and depend on the stated
reference element, exponents and shape-regularity bound. For Lagrange
elements in the existing mesh dimension range $d\ge2$, assume additionally
the Axiom of Choice for the automatic nodal-boundedness application. Then
[[thm-lagrange-point-evaluation-threshold-on-reference-simplex]] supplies
the boundedness hypothesis when $\ell>d/p$; unisolvence of a particular
node set remains a separate hypothesis.

Assume Countable Choice. A Cauchy sequence in $V_h$ therefore has Cauchy coefficient sequences; [F8] gives their limits and the same norm formula gives convergence in $V_h$. Thus $V_h$ is a two-dimensional Hilbert space. Moreover, $\omega_L+\omega_R=2$ is constant, and every $g\in L^2(0,1)$ decomposes as $g=(g-\int_0^1g)+\frac12(\int_0^1g)(\omega_L+\omega_R)$; the first summand lies in $V$ and the second in $V_h$. Thus $X_h=V+V_h=L^2(0,1)$, with the common $L^2$ norm restricting to both spaces. Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

derivations.claim: Lebesgue measure is finite and positive on $[-1,1]$, every relative neighborhood of each point has positive measure, and all bounded-interval polynomial moments are finite. Thus [F1] holds.

Write $p_2(x)=x^2+bx+c$. Orthogonality [F2] to $1$ and $x$, using $\int_{-1}^1 1=2$, $\int x=0$, $\int x^2=2/3$, and $\int x^3=0$ as evaluated by [F5, F6], gives $2/3+2c=0$ and $2b/3=0$. Hence $p_2=x^2-1/3$, and [F3] gives nodes $\pm1/\sqrt3$.

Using the nodes from step 1.2, the corresponding cardinal polynomials are $\ell_+(x)=(x+1/\sqrt3)/(2/\sqrt3)=(1+\sqrt3x)/2$ and $\ell_-(x)=(1/\sqrt3-x)/(2/\sqrt3)=(1-\sqrt3x)/2$. By [F5, F6], their odd terms integrate to zero and their constant terms integrate to one, so [F3] gives both weights equal to $1$.

By [F4], this rule is exact for every polynomial of degree at most three. Using the nodes and weights from steps 1.2–1.3, its value on $x^4$ is $(1/\sqrt3)^4+(-1/\sqrt3)^4=2/9$, whereas [F5, F6] give $\int_{-1}^1x^4dx=2/5$. The absolute error is $2/5-2/9=8/45$.
